tasks.description: Create a class `Animal` with a name attribute and a `speak()` method that prints '{name} makes a sound.'. Create an instance and call speak().
tasks.hint:
`def __init__(self, name): self.name = name` stores the name.
`def speak(self): print(f'{self.name} makes a sound.')`
This is the BASE class — child classes will inherit these.
tasks.walkthrough:
This is the base class. It stores a name and has one method.
Nothing here is about inheritance yet; the next tasks build on it.

tasks.description: Create a class `Cat` that inherits from `Animal`. Override `speak()` to print '{name} says: Meow!'. Create a Cat and call speak().
tasks.hint:
Inheritance syntax: `class Cat(Animal):` — put the parent in parentheses.
Redefining `speak()` in Cat OVERRIDES the parent's version for Cat instances.
`cat = Cat('Whiskers'); cat.speak()` — calls Cat's speak, not Animal's.
tasks.walkthrough:
`class Cat(Animal)` makes Cat inherit from Animal, including its `__init__`.
Cat's own `speak` overrides the parent's, so a Cat meows instead of making a generic sound.

tasks.description: Create a `Dog` class inheriting from `Animal` with its own speak(). Also add a fetch() method. Show that both speak() and fetch() work.
tasks.hint:
Use `super().__init__(name)` in Dog's `__init__` to call Animal's initialiser.
Dog's `speak()` overrides Animal's; `fetch()` is a brand new method only Dog has.
`dog.speak()` + `dog.fetch()` should both work.
tasks.walkthrough:
Dog overrides `speak` and adds a brand new method, `fetch`, that Animal doesn't have.
Its `__init__` just hands the name to the parent with `super()`. Since it adds nothing extra, you could leave that `__init__` out entirely and get the same result.

tasks.description: Create a `Shape` class with a `area()` method returning 0. Create `Circle(Shape)` and `Square(Shape)` subclasses that override area(). Test each.
tasks.hint:
Shape is the base: `def area(self): return 0`
Circle: `self.radius = radius`, `def area(self): return 3.14159 * self.radius ** 2`
Square: `self.side = side`, `def area(self): return self.side ** 2`
tasks.walkthrough:
Shape gives a default `area` that returns 0. Each subclass replaces it with the right formula.
Because they all have an `area` method, you can treat any shape the same way, which is the real benefit.

tasks.description: Use isinstance() to check if a Dog object is an instance of Dog, Animal, and str. Print each result.
tasks.hint:
`isinstance(obj, ClassName)` returns True if `obj` is that type OR a subclass.
A Dog IS an Animal (due to inheritance) — `isinstance(dog, Animal)` → `True`
`isinstance(dog, str)` → `False` — Dog is not related to str.
tasks.walkthrough:
`isinstance` follows the inheritance chain. A Dog is a Dog, and because Dog inherits from Animal, it's also an Animal.
It has nothing to do with strings, so the last check is False.

tasks.description: Create a `Vehicle` class with speed and fuel. Create `Car(Vehicle)` that adds a doors attribute. Create `Truck(Vehicle)` that adds cargo_capacity. Make instances of both and print their attributes.
tasks.hint:
In Car's `__init__`: `super().__init__(speed, fuel)` first, then `self.doors = doors`
In Truck's `__init__`: same pattern with `self.cargo_capacity = capacity`
This avoids duplicating the speed/fuel setup — inheritance handles it.
tasks.walkthrough:
Both child classes call `super().__init__` to set speed and fuel, then store their own extra attribute.
The shared setup lives in one place, Vehicle, instead of being copied into each child.

lesson.intro:
Inheritance lets one class build on another. A `Cat` is an `Animal`, so it gets
everything `Animal` has for free and only adds or changes what's different.
It saves repetition and lets you say "these things are all a kind of X".

sections.heading: A base class and a child class
sections.body:
Put the parent in brackets after the child's name. The child inherits every
method and attribute. If the child defines a method with the same name, that
version wins for child objects. That's called overriding.
sections.output:
Generic makes a sound.
Whiskers says: Meow!

sections.heading: Adding new methods
sections.body:
A child can have methods the parent doesn't. Here `Dog` overrides `speak`
and adds `fetch`. Notice `Dog` has no `__init__` of its own; it uses the
inherited one.
sections.output:
Rex says: Woof!
Rex fetches the ball.

sections.heading: super(): extend the parent's __init__
sections.body:
When a child needs extra attributes, give it its own `__init__`, call
`super().__init__(...)` to let the parent set up its part, then add the rest.

sections.heading: isinstance: is this a kind of that?
sections.body:
`isinstance(obj, Class)` is True if the object was made from that class or
any class that inherits from it. A Dog is an Animal, so both checks pass.
sections.code:
class Animal: pass
class Dog(Animal): pass

d = Dog()
print(isinstance(d, Dog))
print(isinstance(d, Animal))
print(isinstance(d, str))

watch_out: Forgetting `super().__init__(...)` in a child's `__init__`. Then the parent's attributes are never set.
The brackets after the class name hold the parent, not parameters: `class Cat(Animal):`.
Overriding a method replaces it completely. Call `super().method()` inside if you want the parent's behaviour too.
`isinstance` checks the whole chain of parents, `type(obj) == Dog` doesn't.
